entries.label: Flips the sign of one coordinate
entries.description: The student reads the right size for one of the two numbers in the pair but gives it the wrong sign, so they look on the wrong side for that value instead of the right one.

refutation.text_md: You've got the right number for one of the two values, just with the wrong sign — you've treated a negative as if it were positive, or a positive as if it were negative, so you've counted the right distance but in the wrong direction.

Take $q:g10m8s1-1-2:ex8-1-4$: the point you want is at $(-4, -3)$. Keep the $-4$ but flip the $-3$ to $+3$, and you're pointed to a spot on the opposite side of where the point actually is — that's a different point altogether, not the one at $(-4, -3)$.
So once you've read off the $x$ and $y$ values, check the sign on each one on its own: a negative value means counting the other way from where a positive one of the same size would take you.

entries.label: Checks only part of the loop
entries.description: Confirms a shape's naming from a couple of neighbouring vertices whose letters happen to climb correctly, and stops before tracing the rest of the way around.

refutation.text_md: You looked at a couple of vertices sitting next to each other, saw their letters climb correctly, and treated that one climbing pair as enough proof the whole shape is alphabetically named.
In ex8-1-6, shape Y opens exactly like that: it starts L, M, which climbs perfectly — but the very next label jumps straight to Q, skipping right over N, the letter that should really come next.

The same trap appears again in ex8-6-3: shape Y there opens G, H, another correct-looking climb, before jumping to R just one step later. A convincing pair anywhere around the ring doesn't mean the rest of the shape keeps climbing.

So don't stop at one pair. Pick a vertex, trace every single vertex around the shape in the same direction, and check that each label is exactly one letter after the last, all the way back to where you started — only a labelling that survives the whole loop is correctly named.

covers.text: Yes — the first four vertices climb one letter at a time, so the pentagon is correctly named.

verdict.reason: Verified against the three figures directly. Tracing shape Z clockwise in all three figures (top row L-to-R, right column top-to-bottom, bottom row R-to-L, left column bottom-to-top) gives a perfect unbroken climb in every case, confirming the book's rule and this reading convention. The corrective step (trace every vertex the whole way round in one consistent direction) is exactly the book's method, adding nothing beyond it, and it argues specifically against 'stopping after a locally-climbing pair' rather than restating the rule in the abstract.

entries.label: Expects the labels to start at A
entries.description: Judges a shape's naming by whether the first vertex noticed is labelled A, instead of checking that the labels climb one at a time all the way around from wherever they happen to start.

refutation.text_md: You expect the correctly-labelled shape to start at A, the way the alphabet itself starts, so a shape whose first letter you notice is something else — like O, E, or T — looks like it can't be the right one.

But the book's own correct answer never starts at A. In ex8-1-5, shape Z's labels run O, P, Q, R, S, T, A, B, C, D... — climbing one letter at a time and looping from T back round to A, exactly the pattern the rule asks for, even though the run begins at O.

The same holds in ex8-1-6 (the correct shape starts at E) and in ex8-6-3 (it starts at T): across all three questions, the correct shape is never the one that happens to start at A — what makes it correct is that the climb never breaks, wherever it begins.

So don't hunt for A. Pick any vertex, check that each next label is one letter further on (wrapping from T back to A), and follow that all the way round back to your start — if the climb holds the whole way, the shape is correctly named no matter which letter it starts on.

covers.text: No — the naming is wrong because the sequence does not start with the letter A.

verdict.reason: Reconstructed each correct shape (Z) directly from the figures. ex8-1-5: clockwise sequence is O,P,Q,R,S,T,A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J,K,L,M,N — a full climb that wraps T->A, never touching A except mid-cycle; matches the refutation's cited sequence exactly. ex8-1-6: clockwise sequence is C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J,K,L,M,N,O,P,Q,R,S,T,A,B — again a full climb wrapping T->A, and the apex/topmost vertex is E, matching the refutation's claim that this shape 'starts at E'. ex8-6-3: clockwise sequence is R,S,T,A,B,C,...,Q — full climb wrapping T->A, apex vertex T, matching the refutation's claim it 'starts at T'. In every case the correct shape is confirmed correct by the same T->A wraparound climb and none of them opens on A, so the refutation's central point (correctness depends on unbroken climbing, not on starting at A) is accurate and grounded in the actual canonical shapes, not an invented rule.

entries.label: Thinks only one direction counts
entries.description: Believes the vertices must be named going one specific way round the shape (usually clockwise), and doubts or rejects a shape that is correctly named going the other way.

refutation.text_md: You've noticed that the correct shape's labels climb going clockwise, so you've settled on clockwise as the one fixed rule — and a shape labelled the other way round looks wrong on sight.

But the rule the book states doesn't pick a side: a shape is named correctly if its labels climb alphabetically 'either clockwise or anti-clockwise around the shape.' Both directions count equally; clockwise isn't a stricter, separate requirement.

It's true that in ex8-1-5, ex8-1-6 and ex8-6-3 the correct shape always happens to be drawn climbing clockwise — but that's just how those particular diagrams were drawn, not evidence that anti-clockwise fails the rule.

So when you check a shape, follow whichever direction it's drawn in, clockwise or anti-clockwise, and confirm the labels climb by one letter the whole way round in that direction — either direction is a correct naming, as long as you follow it consistently all the way around.

covers.text: No — the labels must be read going anticlockwise instead, since a clockwise reading is never the correct convention.

verdict.reason: The canonical solution's stated rule is verbatim 'alphabetical order, either clockwise or anti-clockwise around the shape' in all three questions, so the refutation quotes the book's own rule accurately rather than inventing one. The corrective advice (follow whichever direction the shape is drawn in, consistently) restates nothing beyond the book's own bidirectional rule.

entries.label: Writes the letters in descending order
entries.description: Traces the shape's vertices in the direction that makes the labels count down instead of climb, ending up with a clean run of consecutive letters in reverse order, without checking that the final order is actually ascending.
entries.signal: The final answer is a straight run of consecutive letters running backwards (descending) rather than forwards (ascending).

refutation.text_md: You're on the right track that a correctly named shape's vertices use consecutive letters as you trace around it — that part of the approach is solid. The mix-up is the direction you traced it in: you went the way that makes the letters count down, rather than the way that makes them climb.

The book's own check, in every one of its naming questions (ex8-1-5, ex8-1-6, ex8-6-3), is to look at a shape and ask whether tracing around it gives the letters in alphabetical order — meaning climbing, like stepping up, not counting down.

Going around the very same four vertices in the opposite direction just reads that climbing order backwards. It still uses the right four letters and still moves one at a time, which is why it can feel right — but the convention specifically calls for the climbing direction, not the counting-down one.

So once you've traced a shape's vertices and written the letters down, check which way they're going: if they climb, you're set; if they count down, retrace the same shape starting from the opposite end, and the letters will climb instead.

verdict.reason: Grounded in the same canonical rule (labels must climb, i.e. ascend, one letter at a time around the shape). Tracing any of the confirmed correct Z shapes in the reverse (anticlockwise-relative) direction produces the same set of consecutive letters read backwards, i.e. a descending run — the exact error this entry describes. It is a distinct, well-defined error (direction of traversal reversed, producing a real descending consecutive run) rather than a restatement of the checking method, and the fix (retrace from the opposite end) is the book's own convention applied correctly.

entries.label: Judges the triangle from the sketch, not the calculation
entries.description: Looks at how the triangle appears in a rough sketch of $P$, $Q$ and $R$ and calls it equilateral because it looks fairly even all round, instead of computing and comparing the three side lengths with the distance formula.

refutation.text_md: You looked at the sketch of $\triangle PQR$ — it comes out looking roughly even all round — and went with equilateral. Sketching the triangle first is exactly what the book asks you to do; the slip is stopping at the picture instead of using it to check a calculation.

The book always settles a triangle's type by calculating every side, not by eye. Here: $PQ=\sqrt{(5-1)^2+(1-3)^2}=\sqrt{16+4}=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt5\approx4.47$, $QR=\sqrt{(1-1)^2+(3-(-2))^2}=\sqrt{0+25}=5$, and $PR=\sqrt{(5-1)^2+(1-(-2))^2}=\sqrt{16+9}=\sqrt{25}=5$. $PQ$ does not match the other two, so all three sides are not equal — the triangle cannot be equilateral, however even the sketch looks.

Whenever you're asked to name a triangle from its coordinates, calculate all three side lengths first and only then compare the numbers: three matches is equilateral, exactly two matches (as here, $QR=PR=5$) is isosceles, and no matches is scalene.

verdict.reason: Canonical q:ex8-6-39a gives PQ=√((5-1)²+(1-3)²)=√20=2√5≈4.47, QR=√((1-1)²+(3-(-2))²)=√25=5, PR=√((5-1)²+(1-(-2))²)=√25=5, so QR=PR≠PQ → isosceles (book answer B). The refutation reproduces these three values exactly and correctly, correctly shows PQ breaks an all-equal reading, and correctly identifies QR=PR as the matching pair. The described error — reading 'looks fairly even all round' off the sketch as equilateral instead of computing — is a real, book-grounded failure mode: the book's own method (and its caution b03156 on sketching) is to sketch first, then verify by calculation, and the error is exactly skipping the second half. The closing rule (3 matches=equilateral, 2=isosceles, 0=scalene) is a direct restatement of the classification the book's own worked examples use (e.g. ex8-6-39a: two sides equal → isosceles; ex8-6-36c: four sides equal → square), not outside content.

entries.label: Loses a sign subtracting a negative coordinate
entries.description: When a coordinate is negative, simplifies a subtraction like $3-(-2)$ straight to $3-2$ instead of $3+2$, so a genuine match between two side lengths disappears and the triangle looks like it has three different sides.

refutation.text_md: You're subtracting $R$'s $y$-coordinate, $-2$, and only one of its two negative signs made it into the calculation, so $3-(-2)$ landed as $3-2$ rather than $3+2$. It's an easy line to lose, especially sitting among simpler single subtractions in the same question.

It matters here because $R(1,-2)$ appears in both $QR$ and $PR$. Done in full: $QR=\sqrt{(1-1)^2+(3-(-2))^2}=\sqrt{0+5^2}=5$ and $PR=\sqrt{(5-1)^2+(1-(-2))^2}=\sqrt{4^2+3^2}=5$ — they genuinely match. Drop the sign the same way in both, though, and $3-(-2)$ becomes $1$ so $QR\to\sqrt{0+1}=1$, while $1-(-2)$ becomes $-1$ so $PR\to\sqrt{16+1}=\sqrt{17}\approx4.12$ — now nothing lines up with $PQ\approx4.47$ either, and the triangle looks scalene when two of its sides are really equal.

Whenever a coordinate is negative, write the subtraction out before simplifying — $y_1-y_2$ with $y_2=-2$ is $y_1-(-2)=y_1+2$ — and square only after that sign is settled. Get that right on both $QR$ and $PR$ and the match between them shows up correctly.

verdict.reason: Canonical values are QR=5 and PR=5 (matching), with PQ=2√5≈4.47. Applying the described slip consistently — treating y1-(-2) as y1-2 rather than y1+2 — to both occurrences of R's y=-2 gives QR→√(0+1²)=1 and PR→√(4²+(-1)²)=√17≈4.12, which the refutation computes correctly and which now differ from each other and from PQ≈4.47, producing an apparent scalene triangle where two sides are genuinely equal. The arithmetic in both the 'correct' and 'erroneous' branches checks out exactly against the canonical method (same distance formula, same coordinates), and the corrective instruction (write y1-(-2)=y1+2 before squaring) is the book's own method, not new content.

entries.label: Only writes down one root
entries.description: Clears the square root and reaches the quadratic correctly, then writes only one of its two solutions as the final answer, not realising a squared difference gives two values.
entries.signal: Final answer gives only one of the two values the quadratic produces (e.g. "y = 21" alone, no "or") for a question where nothing rules the other value out.

refutation.text_md: You cleared the square root and squared both sides correctly — that part is exactly right. The gap is stopping as soon as you find one value that fits, the way you would for an equation like $2y=6$, which really does have only one answer.

But here the unknown sits inside a squared term, $(y_1-y_2)^2$, and a squared term doesn't point back to a single number. For $R(3, 9)$ and $S(8, y)$ with $d=13$, clearing the square root gives $0=y^2-18y-63=(y+3)(y-21)$ — a genuine quadratic, so it factors into two brackets and two roots.

If you stopped at $y=21$ alone, you'd be leaving out $S(8, -3)$, which is just as real a point: $\sqrt{(3-8)^2+(9-(-3))^2}=\sqrt{25+144}=\sqrt{169}=13$, exactly the distance given. Neither root is more correct than the other unless something else in the question says so.

So once you reach a quadratic, factor it (or take $\pm$ of a square root) and write down both values first, then check each one back in the distance formula, the way the book does for every worked example, before deciding whether to keep one or both.

covers.text: Part of the answer set was not marked

verdict.reason: The error is real and book-supported: the caution box at p.290 explicitly warns that squaring (y1-y2)^2 yields a quadratic with two expected values, and WE02's canonical solution factors 0=y^2-18y-63=(y+3)(y-21) and checks both y=-3 and y=21 back into the distance formula. The refutation reproduces this algebra exactly (verified independently: (3-8)^2+(9-y)^2=169 gives y^2-18y-63=0, factoring to (y+3)(y-21)), and its check of the omitted root y=-3 (sqrt(25+144)=13) is correct. It argues specifically against stopping at one root rather than restating the general method, and its closing caveat ('unless something else in the question says so') correctly avoids contradicting the companion entry about restricted questions.

entries.label: Keeps both roots when the question narrows it down
entries.description: Solves the quadratic and finds both values, then reports both even when the question's figure or a stated condition on the coordinate has already ruled one of them out.
entries.signal: Final answer gives both values with "or" (e.g. "x = 1 or x = -3") for a question that shows a figure fixing the point's location, or states a condition on the coordinate (like "k >= 0"), where the book keeps only one.

refutation.text_md: You solved the quadratic correctly and found the two values it produces — that's real progress, and for a question like $CD=5$ with $C(6, -2)$, $D(x, 2)$, both $x=3$ and $x=9$ really are the final answer. The gap is treating every question that way, even when the question has already told you which one it wants.

Some of this objective's questions add a picture or a stated condition alongside the algebra. For the quadrilateral question, solving gives $k=-11$ or $k=1$, but the question states $k\geq 0$, so $k=-11$ is thrown out before you ever write a final answer, leaving only $k=1$.

For the picture questions, the diagram fixes where the point actually sits: for $A(-1, 3.5)$ and $B(x, 0.5)$, the algebra gives $x=1$ or $x=-3$, but the picture shows $B$ down and to the right of $A$, which is only true at $x=1$ — $x=-3$ would put $B$ down and to the left instead.

So after finding both values algebraically, look back at the question before you answer: is there a figure showing where the point lies, or a condition on the coordinate like $k\geq 0$? If yes, use it to drop the value it rules out. If neither is given, both values stand — check both back in the distance formula and keep them both, the way the book does for $CD=5$.

verdict.reason: The error is real and supported by multiple canonical solutions in this LO's evidence: ex8-6-33b algebraically finds k=-11 or k=1 then drops k=-11 solely because the question states k>=0; ex8-2-3 algebraically finds x=1 or x=-3 then keeps only x=1 because the diagram (confirmed by reading the figure: A(-1,3.5) and B plotted at (1,0.5), i.e. down-and-right of A) fixes B's position. The refutation's worked numbers match the canonical solutions exactly in all three cited cases (CD=5 unrestricted case x=3 or 9, the k>=0 quadrilateral case, and the A/B picture case), and its reasoning is mathematically correct throughout. It specifically targets the 'report both regardless of restriction' error rather than merely restating method, and is scoped narrowly enough (figure or explicit coordinate condition) not to misfire on the unrestricted questions that entry 1 covers.

entries.label: Mismatched subscript order in the gradient formula
entries.description: The student subtracts the $y$-coordinates starting from one point but subtracts the $x$-coordinates starting from the other point, so the top and bottom of the fraction don't use the same point first.
entries.signal: The final gradient has the same magnitude as the canonical answer but the opposite sign.

refutation.text_md: You're finding the change in $y$ and the change in $x$ between the two points, which is the right idea — but you started from a different point in each subtraction: say $y_1-y_2$ on top, while the bottom is still $x_2-x_1$.

That mix flips the sign of the answer, because $y_1-y_2$ is always $-(y_2-y_1)$. Unless the denominator is flipped to match, the whole fraction comes out with the wrong sign even though every number in it is correct.

Take $A(7, 10)$ and $B(-4, 1)$ from the book. The book's method gives $m_{AB}=\frac{y_{2}-y_{1}}{x_{2}-x_{1}}=\frac{1-10}{-4-7}=\frac{-9}{-11}=\frac{9}{11}$. Mixing the order instead — $\frac{y_{1}-y_{2}}{x_{2}-x_{1}}=\frac{10-1}{-4-7}=\frac{9}{-11}=-\frac{9}{11}$ — gives the negative of the true gradient.
So before you substitute, decide which point is $\left(x_1, y_1\right)$ and which is $\left(x_2, y_2\right)$, and keep that same order in both places: $m=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$.

verdict.reason: The error (numerator y1−y2, denominator kept as x2−x1) is exactly the caution at b03177 p.294 warns against, which even states the wrong-formula pattern verbatim: m ≠ (y1−y2)/(x2−x1). Worked against the canonical solution for ex8-3-1a (A(7,10), B(-4,1)): canonical m_AB = (y2−y1)/(x2−x1) = (1−10)/(-4−7) = −9/−11 = 9/11, matching the book's stated answer '9 11'. The refutation's arithmetic for both the correct and mistaken computation is exact: correct gives 9/11, the mismatched-order version gives (10−1)/(-4−7) = 9/−11 = −9/11, i.e. the negative of the true value — verified by hand, not just restated. Algebraically, since y1−y2 ≡ −(y2−y1), keeping the denominator unchanged always negates the result regardless of the specific numbers, so the described signal (same magnitude, opposite sign) is a general and correct consequence of exactly this error, not an accident of the chosen example. The refutation stays inside the book's own method and notation (x1,y1/x2,y2 formula, same worked exercise) and introduces nothing external. It diagnoses the specific error (inconsistent point order between numerator and denominator) rather than just restating the procedure — steps 1–2 name the mistake, steps 3–4 falsify it with the book's own numbers and restate the fix.

entries.label: Takes the rise and the run from different point orders
entries.description: Writing $m=\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$, the student subtracts the two points one way round for the top and the opposite way round for the bottom, so the top and bottom no longer come from the same point pair.
entries.signal: the final answer matches what you'd get solving the same equation with the gradient's sign reversed (using $-m$ in place of the given $m$)

refutation.text_md: You've written a rise and a run for the gradient, and everything from there — the cross-multiplying, the solving — is done correctly. The only slip is that the two points aren't taken in the same order on the top as they are on the bottom.

Take $G(7, -9)$ and $H(x, 0)$ with $m_{GH}=3$. The book's way round gives $\dfrac{0-(-9)}{x-7}=\dfrac{9}{x-7}=3$, so $x=10$. Swap only the top around, to $\dfrac{-9-0}{x-7}=\dfrac{-9}{x-7}$, and setting that equal to $3$ gives $x-7=-3$, so $x=4$ — a different point from the book's $10$.

Subtracting measures how far apart the points are, which is a different question, useful for a length or a gradient but not for finding the point in between.

Whenever the point exactly between two given points is needed, add the $x$'s, add the $y$'s, then halve each sum: $M(x, y) = \left(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}, \frac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right)$, exactly as the book sets it out.
